questions.question: Explain Fletcher checksum approach that is suitable for 8-bit and 16-bit checksum calculation.
questions.solution:
The Fletcher checksum was devised to weight each data item according to its position. Fletcher proposed two algorithms, 8-bit and 16-bit. The 8-bit Fletcher calculates on 8-bit data items and creates a 16-bit checksum; it is calculated over data octets (bytes) and the calculation is done modulo 256 (2^8), meaning intermediate results are divided by 256 and the remainder kept. The algorithm uses two accumulators, L and R: the first simply adds data items together, the second adds a weight to the calculation. The 16-bit Fletcher is similar but is calculated over 16-bit data items, creates a 32-bit checksum, and the calculation is done modulo 65,536.
Flowchart: R = L = 0; for each next 8-bit data item Di, R = (R + Di) mod 256 and L = (L + R) mod 256; when no more data, checksum = L x 256 + R, held as the 16-bit pair [L | R].
questions.breakdown_text: 3M for the explanation + 2M for the flowchart

rubric.point: 8-bit Fletcher works on 8-bit data items modulo 256 and produces a 16-bit checksum; 16-bit Fletcher works on 16-bit data items modulo 65,536 and produces a 32-bit checksum; the scheme weights each data item by its position using two accumulators L and R
Flowchart of the 8-bit Fletcher algorithm: R = L = 0, then R = (R + Di) mod 256 and L = (L + R) mod 256 for each data item, ending with checksum = L x 256 + R

questions.question: A small research laboratory uses a switched Ethernet LAN. Host A (IP N1, MAC L1) and Host B (IP N2, MAC L2, unknown to Host A initially) are on the same Layer-2 network. Host A needs to send an IP packet to Host B. Identify the protocol used to initiate the transmission. Demonstrate with a diagram how the protocol Request is sent by Host A and the Reply packet by Host B, and also the contents of the request and reply protocol.
questions.solution:
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) accepts an IP address from the IP protocol, maps the address to the corresponding link-layer address, and passes it to the data-link layer. Anytime a host or router needs to find the link-layer address of another host or router in its network it sends an ARP request packet. The packet includes the link-layer and IP addresses of the sender and the IP address of the receiver. Because the sender does not know the link-layer address of the receiver, the query is broadcast over the link using the link-layer broadcast address.
ARP request (broadcast): carried in a multicast/broadcast frame with destination B (broadcast address) and source A; the ARP request carries hardware type 0x0001, protocol type 0x0800, hardware length 0x06, protocol length 0x04, operation 0x0001, sender L1 and N1, target all-0s and N2.
ARP reply (unicast): frame from B to A with destination A and source B; the ARP reply carries operation 0x0002, sender L2 and N2, target L1 and N1 - 'I am the node and my link-layer address is L2'.

rubric.point: Identifies ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) as the protocol that maps the known IP address to the unknown link-layer address
ARP request: broadcast over the link because the sender does not know the receiver's link-layer address, carrying sender L1/N1 and target N2 with the target hardware address all 0s
ARP reply: unicast from B back to A, carrying B's link-layer address L2 so that A can now frame the packet

notes: Both diagram items are marked as figures: the scheme awards 2+2 explicitly for diagrams, so the evidence for them is a drawing and the human tier decides them.

questions.question: Compare and contrast byte-oriented and bit-oriented protocols. Apply bit stuffing to bit-stuff the following frame payload: 0001111111001111101000111111111110000111. Unstuff the following frame payload: 0001111100000111110111010011101111 1000001111.
questions.solution:
In character-oriented (byte-oriented) framing, the data carried are 8-bit characters from a coding system such as ASCII. The header, which normally carries the source and destination addresses and other control information, and the trailer, which carries error-detection redundant bits, are also multiples of 8 bits. To separate one frame from the next, an 8-bit (1-byte) flag is added at the beginning and end of a frame. [1M]
In bit-oriented framing, the data section of a frame is a sequence of bits to be interpreted by the upper layer as text, graphic, audio, video and so on. In addition to headers (and possible trailers), a delimiter is still needed to separate one frame from the other. Most protocols use a special 8-bit pattern flag, 01111110, as the delimiter to define the beginning and the end of the frame. [1M]
Bit stuffing: whenever five 1s are followed by a 0 in the original data, a 0 is stuffed after five consecutive 1s so the flag pattern can never appear inside the payload. [1.5M]
Bit unstuffing: scan for the pattern 11111 0 and remove the 0. After removing every stuffed 0 the unstuffed sequence is recovered. [1.5M]
questions.breakdown_text: byte-oriented 1M + bit-oriented 1M + bit stuffing 1.5M + bit unstuffing 1.5M

rubric.point: Byte/character-oriented framing carries 8-bit characters, with header and trailer also multiples of 8 bits, and an 8-bit flag at each end of the frame
Bit-oriented framing carries an arbitrary sequence of bits and uses the special 8-bit flag 01111110 as the delimiter
Applies bit stuffing correctly: after five consecutive 1s a 0 is stuffed, so the flag pattern cannot occur inside the payload
Applies bit unstuffing correctly: scan for 11111 followed by 0 and remove that 0

notes: NO `exact` VALUES ON THE BIT STRINGS, DELIBERATELY. The stuffed and unstuffed payloads are 40+ bit strings transcribed by eye from a skewed scan. If one character of that transcription is wrong, an exact match would score every correct student zero, and the error would be invisible. The rule being applied - five 1s then a stuffed 0 - is what is marked, and the strings live in `solution` for a human to compare against.
The stuffed and unstuffed strings should be re-checked against the original PDF before any student is failed on this part.

questions.question: Identify the media access protocol where the stations consult one another to find which station has the right to access the medium. Demonstrate with neat diagrams the protocol where the primary station has all the control of the medium access.
questions.solution:
In controlled access, the stations consult one another to find which station has the right to send; a station cannot send unless it has been authorized by other stations. [Identify 1M]
Polling works with topologies in which one device is designated as a primary station and the other devices are secondary stations. All data exchanges must be made through the primary device even when the ultimate destination is a secondary device. The primary device controls the link; the secondary devices follow its instructions. It is up to the primary device to determine which device is allowed to use the channel at a given time. [Diagram 1M]
Select: the select function is used whenever the primary device has something to send. The primary controls the link, so if it is neither sending nor receiving it knows the link is available. What it does not know is whether the target device is prepared to receive, so it must alert the secondary to the upcoming transmission and wait for an acknowledgment of the secondary's ready status. Before sending data the primary creates and transmits a select (SEL) frame, one field of which includes the address of the intended secondary. [1.5M]
Poll: the poll function is used by the primary to solicit transmissions from the secondary devices. When the primary is ready to receive data it must ask (poll) each device in turn if it has anything to send. When the first secondary is approached it responds either with a NAK frame if it has nothing to send, or with data if it does. If the response is negative the primary polls the next secondary in the same manner until it finds one with data to send. When the response is positive the primary reads the frame and returns an acknowledgment (ACK frame), verifying its receipt. [1.5M]

rubric.point: Identifies controlled access (polling) as the protocol in which stations consult one another and a station cannot send unless authorized
Diagram of the select and poll exchanges between the primary and the secondary stations
Select: used when the primary has something to send; it transmits a SEL frame naming the intended secondary and waits for an acknowledgment of ready status before sending data

Poll: used when the primary is ready to receive; it asks each secondary in turn, receiving a NAK if that station has nothing to send or a data frame if it does, and returns an ACK on a positive response

questions.question: A digital communication system uses NRZ-I and Manchester line coding schemes to transfer 10-Mbps data. (a) Calculate the average signal rate and minimum bandwidth for both schemes. (b) Draw the NRZ-I and Manchester waveform for the bit sequence 1 0 1 1 0 0 1. (c) Analyze the behaviour of both schemes with respect to baseline wandering and self synchronization.
questions.solution:
(a) NRZ-I: average signal rate Savg = c x N x (1/r) with c = 1/2, so Savg = N/2 = 500 kbaud, and minimum bandwidth Bmin = N/2 = 500 kHz. Manchester: c = 1, r = 1/2, so Savg = N = 10 Mbaud and Bmin = N = 10 MHz.
(b) NRZ-I: the level inverts on a 1 and stays on a 0 (next bit 0 - no inversion; next bit 1 - invert the previous level). Manchester: 0 is a high-to-low transition in the middle of the bit, 1 is a low-to-high transition, giving a transition in every bit.
(c) In NRZ-I the baseline wandering problem occurs only for a long sequence of 0s; if the long sequence of 0s can be eliminated, baseline wandering is avoided. The synchronization problem likewise exists for a long sequence of 0s in NRZ-I. In Manchester there is no baseline wandering and no synchronization problem, because every bit carries a mid-bit transition.
questions.breakdown_text: Part A-2+2M  Part B-2+2M  Part C-1+1M

rubric.point: NRZ-I: average signal rate Savg = N/2 = 500 kbaud and minimum bandwidth Bmin = N/2 = 500 kHz
Manchester: average signal rate Savg = N = 10 Mbaud and minimum bandwidth Bmin = N = 10 MHz
NRZ-I waveform for 1 0 1 1 0 0 1: the level inverts on each 1 and is held on each 0
Manchester waveform for 1 0 1 1 0 0 1: a mid-bit transition in every bit, low-to-high for 1 and high-to-low for 0
NRZ-I suffers baseline wandering and loses synchronization on a long sequence of 0s
Manchester has no baseline wandering and no synchronization problem, because every bit carries a transition

notes: The scheme's worked answer for parts (a) and (b) is a photograph of handwriting pasted into the document rather than typed text. The values above (500 kbaud / 500 kHz for NRZ-I, 10 Mbaud / 10 MHz for Manchester) were read from that photograph and are consistent with the standard formulas, but VERIFY against the PDF if a student disputes this question.

questions.question: i) Describe the working of CSMA/CD protocol with example. ii) Assume that there are only two stations, A and B, in a bus CSMA/CD network. The distance between the two stations is 2000 m and the propagation speed is 2 x 10^8 m/s. If station A starts transmitting at time t1: a. Analyze if the protocol allows station B to start transmitting at time t1 + 8 us? If yes, justify. b. Analyze if the protocol allows station B to start transmitting at time t1 + 11 us? If yes, justify.
questions.solution:
i) CSMA does not specify the procedure following a collision. Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD) augments the algorithm to handle the collision: a station monitors the medium after it sends a frame to see if the transmission was successful; if so the station is finished, but if there is a collision the frame is sent again. In the example, at time t1 station A executes its persistence procedure and starts sending the bits of its frame. At time t2 station C has not yet sensed A's first bit, so C executes its persistence procedure and starts sending, and its bits propagate both left and right. The collision occurs some time after t2. Station C detects the collision at t3 when it receives A's first bit and immediately aborts. Station A detects the collision at t4 when it receives C's first bit and also aborts. A transmits for the duration t4 - t1 and C for t3 - t2. [Diagram 2M, explanation 4M]
ii) One-way propagation delay = distance / speed = 2000 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.00001 s = 10 us, so A's first bit reaches B at t1 + 10 us.
a. If B starts at t1 + 8 us: A's signal has not yet arrived (it arrives at t1 + 10 us), so B senses the channel idle and CSMA allows it to start transmitting. When A's signal arrives at t1 + 10 us it collides with B's transmission; B detects the collision immediately, sends a jam and aborts. A detects the collision only after B's signal propagates back: B started at t1 + 8 us and its earliest signal reaches A at t1 + 8 + 10 = t1 + 18 us. Both stations then follow the CSMA/CD collision handling - jam, stop, wait a random backoff, retransmit. [2M]
b. If B starts at t1 + 11 us: A's signal has already arrived at B (it arrived at t1 + 10 us), so B senses the channel busy and must defer - CSMA does not allow B to start transmitting then. No collision occurs; B waits until it senses the channel idle before attempting to transmit. [2M]

rubric.point: Diagram of the CSMA/CD collision: the two stations' transmissions, the point where the collision occurs, and each station's collision-detection and abort times

Explains CSMA/CD: a station monitors the medium while sending, and on detecting a collision it aborts and resends; the worked example shows each station detecting the collision only when the other's first bit reaches it
At t1 + 8 us B senses the channel idle because A's signal has not yet arrived (it arrives at t1 + 10 us), so B is allowed to transmit and a collision follows
At t1 + 11 us A's signal has already arrived, so B senses the channel busy, must defer, and no collision occurs

steps: A's first bit reaches B at t1 + 10 us
a start before t1 + 10 us sees an idle channel; a start after it sees a busy channel
chain.carry_forward: Both sub-answers hang off the single propagation delay of 10 us. A student who computes that delay wrongly will answer both (a) and (b) consistently with their own value; credit the reasoning where the comparison against their own delay is correct, and charge the error once, at the step where the delay is computed.

questions.question: A virtual-circuit connection must be established between host A and host B through two switches S1 and S2. Link A->S1: 2 Mbps, 600 m. Link S1->S2: 1.5 Mbps, 1200 m. Link S2->B: 4 Mbps, 400 m. Packet size for all packets (setup, ack, data, teardown) is 500 bytes. Speed of signal in copper/fibre = 2 x 10^8 m/s. Switch processing delay S1: 1 ms, S2: 1.5 ms. One data packet of 500 bytes is sent. Compute i) round-trip setup delay, ii) per packet delay, iii) total end-to-end time.
questions.solution:
A 500-byte packet is 4000 bits.
Transmission delays: A->S1 Tt1 = 4000 / (2 x 10^6) = 2 ms; S1->S2 Tt2 = 4000 / (1.5 x 10^6) = 2.67 ms; S2->B Tt3 = 4000 / (4 x 10^6) = 1 ms.
Propagation delays: Tp1 = 600 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.003 ms; Tp2 = 1200 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.006 ms; Tp3 = 400 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.002 ms.
i) Round-trip setup delay = 2 x [ sum(Tt + Tp) + S1 processing + S2 processing ] = 2 x [ (2 + 0.003) + (2.67 + 0.006) + (1 + 0.002) + 1 + 1.5 ] = 2 x 8.181 = 16.362 ms.
ii) Per packet delay (data transmission) = sum(Tt + Tp) = (2 + 0.003) + (2.67 + 0.006) + (1 + 0.002) = 5.681 ms per packet.
iii) Total end-to-end time = round-trip setup + data transfer + teardown = 16.362 + 5.681 + 8.181 = 30.224 ms.
questions.breakdown_text: Transmission delay calculation-2M  propagation delay calculation-2M  i)-2M  ii)-2M  iii)-2M

rubric.point: Transmission delays computed from packet size over bandwidth: 2 ms, 2.67 ms and 1 ms for the three links (500 bytes = 4000 bits)
Propagation delays computed from distance over signal speed: 0.003 ms, 0.006 ms and 0.002 ms
Round-trip setup delay = 2 x (sum of transmission and propagation delays plus both switch processing delays) = 16.362 ms
Per packet delay = sum of transmission and propagation delays = 5.681 ms per packet
Total end-to-end time = setup + data transfer + teardown = 30.224 ms

steps: propagation delay per link = distance / (2 x 10^8)
round-trip setup = 2 x (sum of all delays + both processing delays)
per-packet delay = sum of transmission and propagation delays
chain.carry_forward: Every one of the five items is computed from the same six delays. A student who converts 500 bytes to bits wrongly, or drops a processing delay, will carry that single error into the round-trip, per-packet and total figures - three items, six marks, for one slip. Charge it once at the step where it happens and mark the later items against the student's own running values.

notes: The worked solution on this page is a photograph of handwriting pasted into the scheme, and some digits are hard to resolve. The figures above (16.362, 5.681, 30.224) are what that photograph shows and they reconcile arithmetically with the stated link parameters. VERIFY against the PDF before failing a student on a near-miss value.
The scheme's total (iii) adds a teardown phase of 8.181 ms that the question does not explicitly ask about. Marked as printed.

questions.question: A sender wants to transmit the dataword 1101011011 using Cyclic Redundancy Check CRC(n,k). The generator polynomial is represented by the bit pattern 10011. (a) Determine the number of bits in the codeword and redundant bits. Write the augmented message used for division. (b) Perform the CRC binary division and compute the remainder. (c) Determine the final transmitted frame (dataword + CRC). (d) Demonstrate how the receiver verifies whether the received frame contains an error if MSB is flipped.
questions.solution:
CRC(n, k): k = 10 bits, r = 4 and n = 14, so CRC(14, 10). The generator 10011 has degree 4, so 4 redundant bits are needed.
(a) Append 4 zeros to form the augmented message: 11010110110000.
(b) Divide the augmented message by 10011 using XOR at each aligned 1:
  Step 1 - align at position 0, XOR: dividend 11010110110000, divisor 10011, result 01001110110000.
  Step 2 - next 1 at position 2, XOR shifted divisor: result 00000010110000.
  Step 3 - next 1 at position 6, XOR shifted divisor: result 00000000101000.
  Step 4 - next 1 at position 8, XOR shifted divisor: result 00000000001110.
  Remainder = last 4 bits = 1110.
(c) Final transmitted frame = dataword + remainder = 11010110111110.
(d) The receiver divides the received frame by the same generator 10011. If the remainder is 0000 there is no error; for this (uncorrupted) case the remainder is 0000.

rubric.point: k = 10, r = 4 and n = 14 (CRC(14,10)), and the augmented message is the dataword with 4 zeros appended: 11010110110000
Performs the CRC binary division by 10011 with XOR at each aligned 1 and reaches remainder 1110
Final transmitted frame = dataword followed by the CRC remainder = 11010110111110
The receiver divides the received frame by the same generator 10011; a remainder of 0000 means no error, and a non-zero remainder signals one

steps: generator 10011 has degree 4, so r = 4 and n = k + r = 14
append r zeros to the dataword to form the augmented message
divide by the generator using XOR to get the 4-bit remainder 1110
transmitted frame = dataword followed by the remainder
the receiver re-divides; remainder 0 means no error
chain.carry_forward: Parts (b), (c) and (d) all follow from the augmented message in (a). A student who appends the wrong number of zeros produces a wrong remainder and a wrong frame from one mistake - 7.5 marks for one slip. Mark (c) against the student's own remainder from (b), and (d) against their own frame from (c).

notes: The remainder 1110 and the frame 11010110111110 were re-derived independently from the dataword 1101011011 and the generator 10011, and agree with the scheme.

DEFECT IN THE SCHEME: part (d) asks the student to demonstrate the receiver check *if the MSB is flipped*, which should produce a NON-ZERO remainder. The scheme's answer describes the uncorrupted case and states 'for this case, the remainder is 0000'. The question and its answer are about different cases. A student who correctly shows a non-zero remainder for the flipped-MSB frame is answering the question as asked and must not be marked down against the scheme's text. VERIFY with the examiner.
